requirements.requirement: Serve the inventory application over TCP port 8181 on node1
requirements.summary: A systemd-managed Python HTTP server (inventory-app.service) was created, enabled, and confirmed listening on *:8181 via `ss`, with curl against $NODE_IP:8181 returning the inventory JSON payload. This was verified both before and after the mandatory restart, confirming persistence across reboot.

requirements.requirement: Mandatory access control (AppArmor) remains in enforcing mode while the app is set up and serving
requirements.summary: AppArmor was confirmed as the node's MAC system (no SELinux present). aa-status was checked at multiple points — before app creation, immediately after the service was brought up, immediately before restart, and after restart — consistently showing 13/13 profiles loaded and in enforce mode, with the apparmor kernel module loaded throughout.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on node1 (pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered service/data/MAC state)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id e4e401d2... with service active/enabled, AppArmor enforcing, port 8181 listening, and curl succeeding. `shutdown -r now` was issued and acknowledged; a subsequent connection attempt failed (node down), and a later attempt succeeded with a new boot_id (5e5b6798...), directly confirming a real reboot. Post-restart checks show the service active/enabled, port 8181 listening, curl returning the inventory JSON, and AppArmor still 13/13 enforcing — matching the fixed after-prepare/after-executor boot-identity cross-check in the lifecycle snapshots (e4e401d2... -> 5e5b6798...).

overall_summary: The executor deployed a systemd-managed Python HTTP server on node1 that serves inventory JSON on TCP 8181, verified reachable via curl both before and after a full restart, while AppArmor remained continuously in enforcing mode (13/13 profiles) throughout setup, serving, and after reboot. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was completed with clear boot-identity change and full recovery of service, port, and MAC state, corroborated by the fixed before/after lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. A transient Python 3.5 compatibility bug caused a temporary service failure during setup but was promptly diagnosed and fixed, leaving no residue in the final state.
limitations: The lifecycle 'listening-sockets' global observations were captured empty (likely bounded/filtered) both before and after, so they could not independently corroborate the port-8181 listener; port evidence instead relies on executor-run `ss` commands.
No indication of file/directory ownership or permission hardening review beyond default root-owned systemd unit deployment, though nothing in the task or evidence suggests this was required.

operational_hygiene.summary: One state-changing misstep occurred during setup: the first server.py used a Python-3.6-only context-manager form of TCPServer, which is incompatible with the node's Python 3.5, causing inventory-app.service to crash-loop and hit systemd's start-limit ('failed' state) in cmd-6fa9b71a46c74eaa, observed via cmd-fc53823e983b4fe0. This was a legitimate bug fix directly tied to satisfying the port-8181 requirement, not an unrelated experiment, and it was fully corrected in cmd-f2189b3f7db44dde (rewrote server.py, ran `systemctl reset-failed`, restarted successfully). The after_executor lifecycle snapshot confirms no residual failed services and a clean final state. No other unnecessary or unbounded mutations were observed; all other commands were either read-only discovery, necessary file/unit creation, or the mandatory restart protocol.
